cells.tense: Questions arrive on their own now, and you are letting them land before you answer.
cells.ask: Write down the next question that shows up, say it out loud, and notice what the saying does to you.
cells.core:
You're letting a thing stay open long enough to actually see it. A question arrives and you sit with it instead of grabbing the nearest answer, and the listening is quiet and it's working. What you do land on tends to hold because of that.

The piece worth noticing is how little certainty you're reaching for. You can say 'I don't know yet' and let it stand. That's the engine. Keep feeding it: take one live question and say it to a person who hasn't already agreed with you, in your own words, before you've sorted it out. What they do with it isn't the point. The point is that the question gets to exist outside your head.
cells.sheetLine: You sit with the question long enough for the answer to be real.
cells.verb: Listening, questioning, and turning things over with fresh curiosity.
cells.place: The room where what you already are, without the polish or the audience, is allowed to be seen.

cells.tense: You are bracing for a version of this where the answer comes out clean, and that version keeps sliding out ahead of you.
cells.ask: Pick one question you've been rehearsing and ask it today in the roughest words you've got.
cells.core:
You're turning something over before it's had a chance to be said. The question gets held up, checked for the right angle, compared to a cleaner version, and the checking has become the work. Curiosity that used to open a thing now gets spent closing it. What you're reaching for is the moment you look certain, and that moment keeps moving ahead of where you stand.

Meanwhile the real asking is right here, unpolished. You already sense what you notice before you've built the case for it. So let this next question be unfinished in front of someone. Ask it the way you'd ask a friend, not a panel. The value is in the question getting spoken while it's still live and you're still inside it.

cells.tense: The wondering has gone quiet, and you are still standing at the door you closed behind you.
cells.ask: Name one small thing you used to wonder about and spend five minutes looking into it, alone, without telling anyone.
cells.core:
You know how to ask, but the asking stopped. Turning something over feels like exposure, so you handle what's in front of you instead of wondering about it. That works, and it leaves the part of you that learns sitting off to the side, waiting to be invited back in.

What gets it moving isn't more effort at wanting to know. Pick something small and let yourself be a beginner at it. No stakes, no one watching, no result to report. Five minutes is enough. The appetite didn't leave. It just stopped being fed. Give it one easy thing to hold and you'll recognise it again before you've had to name it.
cells.sheetLine: The curiosity didn't go anywhere. You stopped giving it anything to hold.

cells.tense: You are asking questions that shape what gets talked about around you, and filing it under paying attention.
cells.ask: Catch one moment today where your question turned a conversation, and say to yourself, plainly: that was mine.
cells.core:
You ask before you decide, and the people near you answer. It moves what gets discussed, what gets taken seriously, what gets dropped. That has been happening. The only piece missing is the admission. You keep describing it as listening, as being present, as not having an angle.

But the angle is there, and it isn't a flaw. Your questions are a kind of steering, and they stay unowned only because you haven't named it. What's yours is the thing you decide is worth wondering about. Claiming that isn't arrogance. It's accuracy. When the next question lands and turns the room, don't file it under being attentive. File it under being you.
cells.sheetLine: You ask the questions that move the room. That part is yours.
